text:
2026 Gold Glove Award finalists revealed
October 14th, 2026
MLB.com
The 2026 Rawlings Gold Glove Award finalists were announced on Wednesday, with the winners set to be unveiled on ESPN on Sunday, Nov. 1.
Each league has three finalists at each position, including the utility spot, which was awarded for the first time in 2022.
A complete guide to baseball's 2026 awards season
To determine the winners at the nine standard positions, 30 MLB managers and up to six coaches from each team vote from a pool of players in their league, excluding players from their own team. These votes comprise 75% of the selection total, with the SABR Defensive Index counting for the other 25%.
For the utility position, Rawlings collaborated with SABR to create a specialized defensive formula separate from the traditional selection process.
All-time Gold Glove winners
The Blue Jays and Cubs each have five nominees, the most of any club. The Braves, D-backs, Rangers and Royals have four apiece.
Here are the 2026 Gold Glove Award finalists. Each position’s finalists are listed in alphabetical order.
American League
Pitcher
Tanner Bibee
, Guardians
Jacob deGrom
, Rangers
José Soriano
, Angels/Blue Jays
None of these three pitchers has taken home a Gold Glove Award, making for an exciting competition. Looking at the advanced metrics, Bibee has the edge in both Statcast’s
Outs Above Average
(+6) and
Defensive Runs Saved
(+5). Bibee’s and Soriano’s clubs, the Guardians and Blue Jays, have been heavily featured in this award this decade. Shane Bieber won for Cleveland in 2022, and José Berríos won for Toronto the following year.
Catcher
Dillon Dingler
, Tigers
Brandon Valenzuela
, Blue Jays
Austin Wells
, Yankees
Dingler has a strong case for the best all-around catcher in baseball, in no small part due to his elite defense. Dingler’s +17
Fielding Run Value
(per Statcast) ranked
tops among all catchers
and was tied for third best among any defenders. He also led catchers with a +22.1 Defensive Rating, via FanGraphs. Dingler took home Gold Glove honors in 2025, so he’s looking to make it two straight years.
Alejandro Kirk has long been one of the best defensive catchers in baseball and was joined by Valenzuela to make a dynamic duo in ‘26. In just 91 games as a rookie, Valenzuela ranked as a top five catcher in terms of Run Value (+11) and Defensive Rating (+13.6). Valenzuela excelled both at framing and throwing runners out.
Wells has consistently been one of the better defensive catchers in baseball during his time in the Majors. He had a +10 Run Value in 2026, after posting a +12 figure in both 2024 and ‘25. Wells is an excellent pitch framer and also blocks pitches in the dirt with the best of them.
First base
Vladimir Guerrero Jr.
, Blue Jays
Vinnie Pasquantino
, Royals
Christian Walker
, Astros
Guerrero’s progression into one of the better defensive first basemen is a fascinating part of his journey. Whereas he was consistently below average for much of his career, Vlad Jr. flashed his newfound level of defense in the 2025 playoffs and had a career-best defensive season across the board in 2026. Guerrero is looking for his second award after winning it in 2022.
Pasquantino was solid on both sides of the ball in 2026 and improved his defense after his metrics were down in ‘25. He’s looking to become the first Royals first baseman to win the award since Eric Hosmer in 2017.
Walker is no stranger to the Gold Glove Award -- he won it in three straight years for the D-backs from 2022-24. He’s well established as one of the best defensive first basemen of his era and he’s still going strong.
Second base
Michael Massey
, Royals
Chase Meidroth
, White Sox
Cole Young
, Mariners
A Gold Glove winner in the Minor Leagues back in 2021 as the best defensive second baseman in all of the Minors, Massey is an MLB Gold Glove finalist for the first time in 2026. The Kansas City infielder proved his worth with +11 OAA, behind only Jazz Chisholm Jr. (+15) for the most among AL second basemen.
While Massey had the edge in OAA, it was Meidroth who led all AL second basemen with a +10 FRV. Meidroth spent a majority of his time at shortstop as a rookie in 2025 (and still graded out as a plus defender in limited action there in ’26), but he proved to be excellent at the keystone in his second season.
Get the latest from the Pirates
Have the latest news, ticket information, and more from the Pirates and MLB delivered right to your inbox.
Different metrics had considerably different opinions of Young’s defense in 2026. The Mariners second baseman was credited with +16 DRS -- tied for eighth in MLB -- but was tied for 35th of 42 qualifying players at his position with -5 OAA.
Third base
Caleb Durbin
, Red Sox
Brooks Lee
, Twins
Nick Loftin
, Royals
Durbin took a step up defensively in 2026 after being traded to the Red Sox from the Brewers. After accruing +1 OAA during his 2025 rookie season, he racked up +6 OAA in ’26 and led all AL third basemen with +13 DRS. Across MLB, only Alex Bregman and Matt Chapman (both at +15) had more.
A position change turned out to be huge for Lee’s glove. He came up as a shortstop and played there primarily in 2024 and ‘25 (while seeing time at second and third base) but finished with a -3 FRV in both seasons. In 2026, Lee still struggled in limited action at shortstop (-6 OAA) but was excellent (+6 OAA) at third.
Loftin stepped into a bigger role for the Royals with Maikel Garcia hampered by injury and performed admirably, both on offense and defense. He played enough third base to qualify for a Gold Glove at the hot corner while also seeing considerable playing time at second base and in right field. Loftin racked up +6 DRS in 2026, although Statcast was much more critical (-3 OAA, -1 FRV).
Shortstop
Andrés Giménez
, Blue Jays
Taylor Walls
, Rays
Bobby Witt Jr.
, Royals
Giménez won three straight AL Gold Gloves at second base from 2022-24 before former Ranger Marcus Semien beat him out in ’25. After moving to shortstop for Toronto in ’26, he now has a shot to win another Gold Glove at a new position. Giménez finished the season tied with the Cardinals’ Masyn Winn for second among shortstops with +19 OAA.
Opinions on Walls’ defense are considerably split: DRS has him at +21 (tied for third among all players), while Statcast graded him as a poor defender (-2 OAA, -2 FRV). Known for his slick glove at shortstop, Walls is a Gold Glove finalist for the second straight season.
Witt won the previous two AL Gold Gloves at short and is well positioned for a third. His +24 OAA was third in MLB, behind only Pete Crow-Armstrong and JJ Wetherholt, and his +17 FRV was tied with Winn for the most among shortstops. The Royals’ star could make it three straight seasons winning both the Gold Glove and Silver Slugger awards at his position.
Left field
Cody Bellinger
, Yankees
Wyatt Langford
, Rangers
Chandler Simpson
, Rays
Bellinger is vying for his first Gold Glove since 2019, when he won the award as a right fielder for the Dodgers. The 31-year-old led all left fielders with +21 DRS, benefitting from plus range (+6 OAA) and an 93.3 mph average arm strength that ranks in the 94th percentile of MLB.
When healthy, Langford, 24, continued to play sublime defense for the Rangers. He started 87 games in left field and totaled +5 OAA, tied for fourth most among all left fielders. That range stems from a strong jump; only Pete Crow-Armstrong and Ceddanne Rafaela had
better initial reactions
than Langford.
Simpson is one of the
fastest players in baseball
, and he put all that speed to good while roaming the outfield for the AL-best Rays in 2026. Few players improved their range more than Simpson, who led all left fielders with +8 OAA in ‘26 after accruing -5 OAA in ‘25. How did he turn things around? Simpson worked closely with outfield instructor Corey Dickerson to improve his reactions, and now
ranks among the top 10 in jumps
.
Center field
Evan Carter
, Rangers
Steven Kwan
, Guardians
Ceddanne Rafaela
, Red Sox
Carter remained mostly healthy this year for the Rangers, appearing in 140 games in center field. Boosted by elite speed, the 24-year-old totaled +11 OAA in 2026, tied for fourth most among primary center fielders.
For the first time in his five-year career, Kwan started more games in center field (77) than in left (65) in 2026. That’s why the four-time defending Gold Glove Award winner is eligible at a different position this year. Kwan often displayed his plus arm, recording 11 outfield assists – tied for third most in MLB – and taking part in five double plays.
Rafaela isn’t quite on Pete Crow-Armstrong’s level in center field, but he’s pretty close. The 26-year-old ranked second among outfielders with +16 FRV and +17 OAA. Rafaela’s 10 five-star catches led all qualified outfielders, which certainly passes the eye test.
Right field
Wilyer Abreu
, Red Sox
Nathan Lukes
, Blue Jays
Cam Smith
, Astros
By at least one popular metric, Abreu was the best defender in baseball in 2026: His +28 DRS led all MLB players by a wide margin. Statcast doesn’t quite favor Abreu as much, but there’s no doubting the arm of the two-time Gold Glove Award winner. Abreu’s 95.3 mph average arm strength is a top 10 mark among qualified players, and his 13 outfield assists trailed only the Dodgers’ Andy Pages.
Abreu isn’t the only AL right fielder with a cannon. Lukes joined Abreu as one of seven players with 10-plus outfield assists this season. According to Statcast’s arm value metric, Lukes had the
most valuable outfield arm
in the American League.
Smith, 23, has only been a full-time outfielder for two seasons. And in each of those two seasons, he’s been a Gold Glove finalist. He looked more comfortable in right field this year, benefitting from improved range: His +7 OAA ranked in the 91st percentile of MLB and fourth most among primary right fielders.
Utility
José Caballero
, Yankees
Ezequiel Duran
, Rangers
Zach McKinstry
, Tigers
Caballero racked up +12 DRS while moving all around the diamond for the Yankees. He played every defensive position but pitcher, catcher and first base. His 0 FRV is actually the lowest of his career -- his best was +8 as a rookie with the Mariners in 2023 -- but Caballero is still a first-time finalist for a Gold Glove.
Duran racked up 4.4 FanGraphs
WAR
in 2026 thanks in part to stellar defense, tying for sixth in MLB with +17 OAA (including +11 at shortstop). He was a true utility player for Texas, making double-digit appearances at second base, third base, shortstop and all three outfield positions.
Versatility has always been a big part of McKinstry’s career, but 2026 marked the first season since 2021 where his most-played position was in the outfield. He made 62 appearances in right field, 45 at second base, 34 at shortstop and a handful at third base, in left field and in center field. His +15 DRS ranked in the top 15 among all players, and his +12 FRV was tied for 14th.
National League
Pitcher
Michael McGreevy
, Cardinals
Nolan McLean
, Mets
Chris Sale
, Braves
McGreevy became a mainstay in the Cardinals’ starting rotation this year, and his prowess wasn’t limited to dealing from his seven-pitch arsenal. He was also excellent at fielding his position, to the tune of +5 Defensive Runs Saved -- tied for the most among pitchers in MLB.
McLean, meanwhile, got well-deserved notoriety for his strong rookie campaign with the Mets, but he was also right behind McGreevy with +4 DRS. And Sale, a candidate to win his second Cy Young Award, is also a finalist for winning his second Gold Glove Award.
Catcher
Freddy Fermin
, Padres
Gabriel Moreno
, D-backs
Luis Torrens
, Mets
Fermin was well rounded in his defensive excellence this past season, ranking in the 86th percentile or better in Statcast blocks above average (+10, 93rd percentile), caught stealing above average (+6, 97th) and average pop time (1.88 seconds, 86th).
Moreno, who won a Gold Glove Award behind the plate in 2023, had a breakout year for the D-backs that could net him some down-ballot NL MVP votes, also ranked among the top 20% of qualified catchers in blocks above average and caught stealing above average. He was second only to Dingler with +14 Defensive Runs Saved.
Torrens was third among MLB backstops with +12 DRS, and his +10 fielding run value ranked in the 90th percentile.
First base
Ty France
, Padres
Matt Olson
, Braves
TJ Rumfield
, Rockies
France, who is seeking his second career Gold Glove honor after winning at first base in the AL last year, enjoyed a career year at the plate for San Diego but also led MLB first basemen with +15 Defensive Runs Saved.
The first baseman who ranked first in fielding run value, with +12? That would be Olson, who is seeking his fourth Gold Glove Award. And Rumfield, who emerged as a star rookie for the Rockies, proved to be more than an on-base machine (he led the NL with a .390 OBP) -- he finished with +6 DRS.
Second base
Brandon Lowe
, Pirates
Brice Turang
, Brewers
JJ Wetherholt
, Cardinals
Wetherholt impressed both at the plate and in the field as a rookie, but at the keystone position is where he shined brightest, leading all second basemen and even coming in second among all players -- regardless of position -- with +25 Outs Above Average.
Turang, meanwhile, accomplished the same feat in the Defensive Runs Saved department, with +23 to lead second basemen and finish runner-up among all players. If he wins the honor this year, it will be his second Gold Glove Award after he won in 2024 -- he also won the
Platinum Glove Award
for the NL that year.
Lowe was stellar as well, with his +15 OAA tied with Turang and Chisholm for second among second basemen. It was quite the year-to-year turnaround for the 32-year-old, who had the
worst range
among any primary second baseman in 2025.
Third base
Alex Bregman
, Cubs
Max Muncy
, Dodgers
Javier Sanoja
, Marlins
Bregman, who won his first Gold Glove in 2024 in his final year with the Astros, finished with +9 OAA, second among all third basemen behind only the Padres’ Manny Machado (+12). He has shown consistency at the hot corner, grading out as an above-average defender in each of the past seven seasons.
Muncy, by contrast, hasn’t been a plus defender by fielding run value since 2021 (+5), the only previous time he was a Gold Glove finalist. He had a 0 FRV and -1 OAA for the Dodgers in 2026.
Sanoja was the NL’s Gold Glove winner at the utility position in 2025. He continued to play all over the diamond in ’26, but he saw the majority of action at third base this time around. His +6 OAA ranked fourth among NL third basemen, and his +5 FRV was tied for fourth.
Shortstop
Geraldo Perdomo
, D-backs
Dansby Swanson
, Cubs
Masyn Winn
, Cardinals
Winn eyes his second consecutive Gold Glove Award following another strong season with the glove. In fact, his numbers in 2025 (+17 FRV, +21 OAA) are more or less identical to his numbers in ‘26 (+17 FRV, +19 OAA), even though a left thumb fracture limited him to just 136 games. One way Winn got better? His rocket of an arm was even stronger, with 94.4 mph average arm strength
leading all middle infielders
.
Swanson won consecutive Gold Gloves from 2022-23, and his defense ticked back up again in ‘26 after a subpar performance last season. The 32-year-old became more deft at going to his backhand, recording +16 OAA – more than all but three qualified shortstops – and anchoring
one of the game’s all-time great defenses
.
Perdomo set new career highs with +13 FRV and +16 OAA. In fact, through his first five years in the Majors, he accrued just +10 OAA. His evolution into one of baseball’s elite defensive shortstops earns him a spot as a Gold Glove finalist for the first time in his career.
Left field
Jackson Chourio
, Brewers
Ian Happ
, Cubs
Daylen Lile
, Nationals
Chourio’s defense took a massive step forward in 2026, setting career highs with +9 FRV and +7 OAA in his third full big league season. He led NL left fielders in both categories.
Happ eyes his fifth consecutive Gold Glove on the heels of another above-average season in left field. Most of his defensive value comes from his arm; Happ recorded nine outfield assists in 2026, tied for eighth most in MLB.
Lile, a second-year player, drew 124 starts in left field for the Nationals, a year after splitting his time between DH, right field and left field. He handled the role admirably, with above-average range (+1 OAA) and a valuable throwing arm (+1 arm value).
Center field
Pete Crow-Armstrong
, Cubs
Michael Harris II
, Braves
Andy Pages
, Dodgers
Crow-Armstrong is the best defender in baseball. His defense was worth +23 runs, according to FanGraphs’ “
defensive runs
” metric, which paced all players. PCA also led the Majors in Statcast’s fielding run value (+26) and Outs Above Average (+26), with the latter tied for the most OAA by an outfielder in a single season since at least 2016.
Harris II put together the best defensive season of his young career, with career highs in OAA (+14) and fielding run value (+12).
Pages accrued +13 FRV in 2026 – third most among qualified outfielders – in part because of a sensational arm. He led MLB with 14 outfield assists and has recorded double-digit assist totals in consecutive years.
Right field
Carson Benge
, Mets
Corbin Carroll
, D-backs
Seiya Suzuki
, Cubs
Benge, 23, burst onto the scene as an NL Rookie of the Year contender thanks in part to his sublime defense. He was one of seven outfielders to record 10-plus assists and had the
most valuable arm
in baseball, according to Statcast’s Arm Value metric. Benge’s 96.6 mph average arm strength ranked fifth highest in the game.
Few players improved their defense from 2025 to ‘26 as much as Suzuki. The 32-year-old veteran totaled +8 fielding run value this past season after accruing negative FRV in each of his first four big league seasons. Suzuki’s +14 DRS ranked second highest among all right fielders.
Carroll makes up for a subpar arm with fantastic range: He uses elite speed to cover a ton of ground, ranking in the 95th percentile of MLB with +10 OAA. It’s the third consecutive year that Carroll, a Gold Glove finalist last year, finished with double-digit OAA totals.
Utility
Mauricio Dubón
, Braves
Jared Triolo
, Pirates
Ildemaro Vargas
, D-backs
Dubón claimed the 2023 and ’25 AL Gold Gloves at utility for the Astros and continued to play stellar defense after being traded to Atlanta. He mostly split time between shortstop and left field while also appearing at second base, at third base and in center field. Dubón posted +6 OAA at short, +1 at third, +1 in center, 0 at second and -1 in left.
Triolo would also be a repeat winner: He was the NL’s utility Gold Glover in 2024, his second big league season. In 2026, he saw action mostly at shortstop and third base but also made eight appearances at first base, six in right field and even one in center field. Grading out best at third base, Triolo ended the year with +5 DRS overall for Pittsburgh.
Playing primarily first base (74 appearances) and second base (56), Vargas had a +4 FRV, tied with 2022 for the best of his career. He saw enough action at third base, shortstop and left field to qualify for the utility position, marking the first Gold Glove finalist nod of his career.

title:
Pirates Insider: Brandon Lowe, Jared Triolo named Gold Glove finalists. What are their chances of winning? | When the Pirates acquired Brandon Lowe last December, they knew they were getting left-handed power that would play at PNC Park, plus veteran leadership that had been lacking among position players.
Similar to Jake Mangum and Mason Montgomery and how they’ve established themselves in Pittsburgh, Lowe’s defensive turnaround made the
text:
Pirates Insider: What are Lowe, Triolo's chances of winning Gold Gloves?
October 14th, 2026
Jason Mackey
When the Pirates acquired
Brandon Lowe
last December, they knew they were getting left-handed power that would play at PNC Park, plus veteran leadership that had been lacking among position players.
Similar to Jake Mangum and Mason Montgomery and how they’ve established themselves in Pittsburgh, Lowe’s defensive turnaround made the swap with the Rays that much more lopsided.
The sizable and impressive improvements Lowe made at second base were officially recognized Wednesday, as Rawlings announced the 32-year-old as one of three Gold Glove finalists at the position and one of two from the Pirates.
Jared Triolo
, who won a Gold Glove as a utility player in 2024, once again earned utility finalist honors.
“I’ve been pretty happy with how the defense has turned around for this year,” Lowe said. “It’s a testament to the coaching staff here that has helped me out.”
Added manager Don Kelly: “He’s been such a stabilizing force for us all year. The defense has been much, much better than anticipated.”
It would be pretty much impossible for another MLB player to author such a drastic turnaround. Numerically speaking, anyway.
In 2025, Lowe was worth -14
defensive runs saved
, per FanGraphs. Among those who spent at least 600 innings at second base, only Luis García Jr. in Washington fared worse at -17.
Flip ahead to this past season.
Lowe was worth 14 DRS, tied for 15th among all defenders.
"He's done everything we could have hoped for as a player and also in the clubhouse," Pirates general manager Ben Cherington said.
Shortly after the trade was consummated, there was a conversation between infield coach Chris Truby and Lowe about where things stood defensively coming off a down year.
The Pirates thought Lowe could improve. So did Lowe. One important tweak was a pre-pitch bunny hop that Lowe started doing to speed up his footwork.
On top of that, there was seemingly a part of Lowe intent on providing that he wasn’t defensively deficient, that he was capable of holding his own in the field. It all came together nicely — and at a perfect time contract-wise.
“He was pegged with being a better hitter than fielder over his career,” Bubba Chandler said. “He’s an unbelievable hitter, but I think what he’s done in the field is pretty darn good. He’s a heck of a second baseman. He doesn’t really get the credit he deserves. It’s tough when you have JJ Wetherholt and Brice Turang in your division.”
Wouldn’t you know it, those are the two other finalists, as expected, Wetherholt with the Cardinals, Turang for the Brewers.
It’s also not hard to make the case for either of them to win. Wetherholt, for instance, has been worth 25
outs above average
, per Baseball Savant. Turang sits at 16, Lowe 15.
Over at FanGraphs, Turang leads the way with 23 DRS, 10 more than Lowe and Wetherholt.
If you want to use Fielding Run Value, another metric on Baseball Savant, Wetherholt ranks second among all defenders at 23, while Turang (14) also ranks ahead of Lowe (12).
But where Lowe has been most impressive is when you look at the total package after he slashed .260/.331/.493 with 35 home runs and 96 RBIs, accounting for a career-high 5.4 bWAR.
Lowe might come up short to Turang and Wetherholt, but there’s absolutely nothing to be ashamed of when it comes to his season, which included 130 putouts and 363 assists in 554 chances.
It was hugely impactful for the Pirates and extremely respectable for Lowe as a player.
“It’s a testament to how much of a pro he is and how he goes about his business,” Chandler said of Lowe, whose FRV of 12 was surpassed by only 13 MLB players regardless of position. “Dude has had an unbelievable career and unbelievable year.”
The last Pirates second baseman to win a Gold Glove remains Jose Lind in 1992.
As for Triolo, his defense at shortstop was much needed when Konnor Griffin was hurt for two longer stretches. Among NL shortstops with at least 500 innings played at the position, Triolo and Griffin were tied for sixth with 4 DRS.
Triolo logged 260 1/3 innings at third base and totaled 5 DRS, which is one shy of the two other utility finalists: Ildemaro Vargas of the Diamondbacks and Mauricio Dubón of the Braves. Dubón leads with 5 OAA, followed by Vargas (2) and Triolo (1).
What Triolo did on the left side of the infield was largely expected, which is why his roster spot has never really been in doubt, because he adds responsible defense pretty much anywhere he plays.
The frustrating part is obviously a .652 career OPS that teases during the second half of seasons but hasn’t offered much of a consistent threat.
Winners will be announced on ESPN on Nov. 1. Snagging another Gold Glove could make Triolo the first Pirates player to win multiple since Ke’Bryan Hayes (2023 and ’25).

Jason.Mackey@pirates.com
and @JMackey_PGH on X.

title: Best prospect stat from each MLB farm system 2026 | The most important thing for prospects is development: learning how to be a professional, acquiring new skills, sharpening tools or pitches. There often can be bumps in the road along the path to the big leagues, and it's important to note that performance and production in the moment isn't necessarily
text:
Here's one stat from each farm system that caught our eye in 2026
October 14th, 2026
Jim Callis
Jonathan Mayo
The most important thing for prospects is development: learning how to be a professional, acquiring new skills, sharpening tools or pitches. There often can be bumps in the road along the path to the big leagues, and it's important to note that performance and production in the moment isn't necessarily the be-all/end-all in projecting future success.
More from MLB Pipeline
:
•
Top 100 prospects
|
Stats
|
Video
|
Podcast
|
Complete coverage
Sometimes, though, top prospects also put up impressive numbers on that developmental journey and the game is still very much results-based. Below is a standout stat from a prospect in each organization. In many cases, each of these players sat at, or near, the top of their systems not only in the category we chose to highlight, but in many others as well. Not surprisingly, a good amount of these high-performing prospects earned organizational hitting or pitching
prospect of the year
nods a week ago.

AMERICAN LEAGUE EAST
Blue Jays: 36.0 K%
Nolan Perry, RHP (
No. 2
/
MLB No. 90
)
A 12th-round pick in 2022, Perry missed the 2025 season due to Tommy John surgery, but he sure shook off the rust in a hurry while reaching Double-A for the first time in 2026. His strikeout percentage -- he whiffed 117 in 82 2/3 innings -- led the Blue Jays and was fourth among all Minor League pitchers with at least 80 IP. He was also top 10 with his 2.50 ERA, .181 BAA, 1.02 WHIP, 12.7 K/9 and 26.2 K-BB%.
Orioles: .186 BAA
Joseph Dzierwa, LHP (
No. 3
/
MLB No. 69
)
The 6-foot-8 lefty was the Orioles' second-rounder in 2025 out of Michigan State and made the most of his first full season, spending most of it in Double-A. He led all Minor League pitchers with that .186 batting average against, while also topping them with his 0.90 WHIP and finishing second in ERA (2.27).
Rays: 22 HR, 44 SB
Theo Gillen, OF (
No. 2
/
MLB No. 16
)
Gillen was one of only five Minor Leaguers to have a 20-40 season, as he reached Double-A at age 20. The 2024 first-rounder got to his power more consistently and finished the year with a .965 OPS, tops in the Rays organization and 15th among qualified full-season Minor Leaguers.
Red Sox: 32.2 K%
Dylan Brown, LHP (
No. 19
)
Brown ranked second in the Minors in strikeout rate among official qualifiers, a shade behind Marlins left-hander Julio Mendez (32.3 percent), and also topped Red Sox farmhands in ERA (3.46) and strikeouts (143 in 106 2/3 innings between Single-A and High-A) during his pro debut. The 2025 eighth-rounder from Old Dominion has a fastball that tops out at 95 mph but misses bats with command and deception.
Yankees: .358 AVG, 16 HR, 67 RBI
Wilberson De Pena, OF (
No. 13
)
Acquired from the Angels in exchange for Oswald Peraza at the 2025 Trade Deadline, De Pena earned MVP and top prospect accolades in the Rookie-level Florida Complex League after winning the triple crown. He also paced the FCL in slugging (.677), OPS (1.088), hits (81), doubles (20), extra-base hits (38) and total bases (153) while displaying well above-average raw power and flashing plus speed.
AMERICAN LEAGUE CENTRAL
Guardians: .952 OPS
Cooper Ingle, C/OF (
No. 4
)
Ingle was named International League MVP after topping the Triple-A circuit in OPS, wRC+ (151) and walk rate (18 percent). The 2023 fourth-rounder from Clemson is a disciplined hitter with average power and more athleticism than most catchers.
Royals: 1.120 OPS
Angeibel Gomez, OF (
No. 2
/
MLB No. 76
)
We know we have to take Rookie-level Dominican Summer League stats with a grain of salt, but it's hard not to get excited about Gomez, especially after seeing him holding his own at age 17 in the Arizona Fall League. Signed for $2.9 million in January, Gomez led qualified Royals prospects at any level in OPS, SLG (.652) and ISO (.292).

Tigers: 13.5 K%
Max Anderson, 2B/3B (
No. 10
)
We might need to start a "Free the prospect" campaign because it's clear Anderson is ready for a big league shot offensively, but without a clear spot in Detroit for him. He topped all qualified Tigers players with that minuscule strikeout rate, in line with his career numbers, and he also led the system with a 134 wRC+.
Twins: 417 PA
Walker Jenkins, OF (
No. 1
/
MLB No. 13
)
Plate appearances aren’t exactly a new-fangled stat, but it stands out for Jenkins, who has had some issues with staying healthy. The 417 PA combine his Minor League and big league debut totals and represent a career high. When he's been on the field, he's produced, and this year was no different, with his .939 OPS with Triple-A St. Paul giving the Twins confidence to call him up for the first time.
White Sox: 69 XBH
Caleb Bonemer, 3B/SS/OF (
No. 2
/
MLB No. 27
)
Bonemer won Single-A Carolina League MVP honors in his 2025 pro debut, then demonstrated significantly more power in his second pro season. He led the Minor Leagues in extra-base hits while boosting his home run production from 12 to 37 (fifth in the Minors), the result of turning his right-handed swing loose more often and with an improved launch angle, enabling him to hit balls harder and farther. The 2024 second-rounder from a Michigan high school ranks as baseball's best third-base prospect but is
focusing on the outfield in the Arizona Fall League
to expedite his bat to the big leagues.
AMERICAN LEAGUE WEST
Angels: 24.0 K-BB%
Tyler Bremner, RHP (
No. 2
/
MLB No. 42
)
While an early illness limited Bremner's workload in his first full season, the No. 2 overall pick in the 2025 Draft still reached Double-A and led the org (min. 70 IP) not only in K-BB percentage, but also in FIP (3.46) and xFIP (3.51).
Astros: 32 HR, 32 SB
Jason Schiavone, C/OF (
No. 6
)
An 11th-rounder from James Madison in 2024, Schiavone went from hitting .180 in his first full pro season to posting the second-ever 30-30 season by a Minor League catcher in his second while advancing from High-A to Triple-A. He's a study in extremes with high-end exit velocities, patience bordering on passivity but also worrisome swing-and-miss rates (both overall and versus strikes).
A's: .904 OPS
Devin Taylor, OF (
No. 7
)
The A's second-rounder in 2025 began the year in High-A and finished it in Triple-A, producing everywhere he went. He led the system in OPS, and also in wRC+ (129) while finishing with a .308/.411/.493 line and knocking firmly on the big league door.
Mariners: 10.38 K/BB
Kade Anderson, LHP (
No. 1
/
MLB No. 5
)
MLB Pipeline's Pitching Prospect of the Year led the Minors (min. 90 IP) in a host of pitching categories, including ERA (1.06), WHIP (0.64), average-against (.147) and walks (13), but that K/BB rate really stands out. The 2025 No. 3 pick's K/BB was 2.38 more than his closest competitor (fellow Mariner Ryan Sloan).
Rangers: .991 OPS
Sebastian Walcott, SS/3B (
No. 1
/
MLB No. 8
)
Billed as the best Bahamian prospect ever when he signed for $3.2 million in 2023, Walcott likely would have made his big league debut this year at age 20 if he hadn't required internal brace surgery on his throwing elbow in February. But it wasn't a completely lost season, as he showed off his precocious bat and well-above-average power by slashing .325/.401/.590 with 10 homers in 41 games (mostly in Double-A) after returning in mid-July.

NATIONAL LEAGUE EAST
Braves: 26 HR, 56 SB
Eric Hartman, OF (
No. 1
/
MLB No. 38
)
A 20th-round pick out of the western Canadian high school scene, Hartman shot up the Top 100 with his breakout season as the only player in the Minors to turn in a 20-50 campaign. He reached 20-30 in just 71 games, the second-fastest to get there since 2005.
Marlins: 1.72 ERA
Jacob Kisting, RHP (
No. 21
)
Traded from the Twins to the Rays last November for Eric Orze and then to the Marlins in a package for Liam Hicks in July, Kisting broke out by leading the Minors in ERA and ranking second in opponent average (.186) and WHIP (0.91). Drafted in the 14th round out of Bradley in 2024, he operates from a low release height that adds deception, owns a low-90s fastball that plays up with horizontal action and command and keeps batters off balance with two versions of a low-80s changeup.
Mets: 163 K
Jonathan Santucci, LHP (
No. 2
)
The Duke product went in the second round of the 2024 Draft and has steadily pitched his way up the ladder, reaching Triple-A in 2026. He edged Jurrangelo Cijntje of the Cardinals, Cedric De Grandpre of the Braves and Adam Seminaris of the Phillies by one K for the Minor League strikeout crown. He led the Mets organization in K/9 (11.74), K% (30.8) and xFIP (3.73).
Nationals: .463 SLG
Eli Willits, SS (
No. 1
/
MLB No. 6
)
The Nationals made Willits the No. 1 overall pick in 2025, and there were several other clubs that rated him as the best player in the Draft, but the one question was how much power he ultimately would have. An Oklahoma high school product who's the son of former big league outfielder Reggie Willits, he put those concerns to rest by hitting 14 homers and slugging .463 as an 18-year-old climbing from Single-A to Double-A. Guardians outfielder Juneiker Caceres was the only age-18 batting qualifier in full-season ball with a higher slugging percentage (.484).
Phillies: 176 wRC+
Francisco Renteria, OF (
No. 3
/
MLB No. 73
)
Renteria joins Angeibel Gomez as the lone players from the DSL to make this list. Signed by the Phillies last January for $4 million, Renteria earned league MVP honors after hitting .379/.470/.682. That 176 wRC+ led qualified Minor Leaguers at any level, as did his .682 SLG and 1.152 OPS. He topped the Phillies system in batting average, OBP and ISO (.303) as well.
NATIONAL LEAGUE CENTRAL
Brewers: 48 HR
Andrew Fischer, 3B/1B (
No. 5
)
Fischer's 48 homers were the most by a Minor Leaguer since Ron Kittle's 50 in 1982, and he also topped the Minors in slugging (.654), OPS (1.067) and total bases (287) while ranking second in RBI (114) and wRC+ (162). The 2025 first-rounder from Tennessee produces some of the highest exit velocities and launch angles in the Minors, but he also comes with some of the worst contact rates, both overall and against strikes.
Cardinals: .328 AVG, .408 OBP, .591 SLG
Rainiel Rodriguez, C/1B (
No. 1
/
MLB No. 10
)
Rodriguez established himself as the game's premier catching prospect by leading the Double-A Texas League in all three slash stats at age 19 and batting a combined .324/.413/.574 with 27 homers and 11 steals in 115 games between that level and High-A. Signed for $300,000 out of the Dominican Republic in 2024, he still requires some defensive polish, but his bat should make him a star.
Cubs: 127 R, 120 BB, 70 SB
Kane Kepley, OF (
No. 5
)
The Cubs selected Kepley in the 2025 Draft's second round out of North Carolina because he's a classic table-setter with plus hitting ability, speed and center-field defense. In his first full pro season, he led the Minors in runs (the most in a season since 2019), walks (the most since 2015) and steals.
Pirates: 40.4 K%
Seth Hernandez, RHP (
No. 1
/
MLB No. 9
)
The only thing that slowed Hernandez down was an oblique injury that ended his season in July. He led all Pirates pitchers (min. 70 IP) in several categories, including that K%, ERA (2.43), xFIP (3.19) and K-BB% (29.8). That 40.4 percentage was good for third among Minor Leaguers with that many innings, while he finished third in K/9 (14.35), fourth in K-BB% and seventh in xFIP.
Reds: .986 OPS
Carter Graham, 1B (
No. 22
)
An eighth-round pick in 2023, Graham had little to show for his first two full years of pro ball, but he jumped on the prospect radar by finally getting out of A ball and up to Double-A while slashing a combined .300/.421/.565 in 2026. He led the Reds in OPS and wRC+ (151) and all three slash line categories, as well as counting stats like home runs (29) and RBIs (93).
NATIONAL LEAGUE WEST

D-backs Top 30

Acquired from the Phillies last December for Kyle Backhus, Owusu-Asiedu recorded the first 25-25 season ever by a D-backs farmhand. The 6-foot-4, 245-pounder possesses plus raw power and solid speed once he gets going.

MLB No. 4
)
The best offensive prospect in the Minors, De Paula required just 11 big league games to claim a spot on the Dodgers' postseason roster, going 10-for-31 with twice as many walks (11) and as many extra-base hits as strikeouts (five). Signed for $397,500 out of the Dominican Republic in 2022, he won Texas League MVP honors this summer after slashing .303/.401/.547 and topping the Double-A circuit in hits (152), doubles (37), runs (106) and RBI (104).
Giants: 3 straight league pitcher of the year awards

No. 9

Bresnahan earned league pitcher of the year accolades for the third straight season, adding High-A Northwest League hardware to go with awards from the Rookie-level Arizona Complex (2024) and Single-A California (2025) leagues. Padres: Age 20
Ethan Salas, C (
No. 1
/
MLB No. 21
)
At 20, Salas was the youngest player in the MLB playoffs and started three of San Diego's four Division Series games. The top-rated prospect in the 2023 international class, he signed for $5.6 million out of Venezuela before struggling with injuries and getting rushed by the Padres in 2024 and '25. He bounced back to bat .296/.374/.448 with 10 homers and 17 steals in 96 games between Double-A and Triple-A this season and won the

No. 5

Arguelles signed in January 2024 for $700,000, and in his two most recent main stops -- the DSL in 2025 and the Arizona Complex League this year -- he's hit over .400. He hit .422 in the Dominican, earning league MVP honors, then hit .402 in the ACL to earn another MVP award before getting promoted to full-season ball for the first time. He'll bring a .344/.434/.518 career line with him into the 2027 season.

text:
Where does Pittsburgh's farm system stand entering 2027?
October 13th, 2026
Aiden Stepansky
This story was excerpted from Aiden Stepansky's Pirates Beat newsletter. To read the full newsletter,
click here
. And
subscribe
to get it regularly in your inbox.
PITTSBURGH -- The Pirates' farm system produced plenty of ammo in 2026 to help build an 11-win improvement for the Major League club. Top prospect Konnor Griffin emerged as the everyday shortstop while rookie Bubba Chandler started 30 games in the rotation.
Further additions came from Esmerlyn Valdez, who homered 17 times and won NL Rookie of the Month for July, and catcher Rafael Flores Jr. also produced a strong year. Who could be up next for Pittsburgh?
COMPLETE PIRATES PROSPECT COVERAGE
Pirates Top 30 prospects
2026 prospect stats
Draft pick stats
Highlights
There are obvious top prospects like Seth Hernandez, Edward Florentino, Murf Gray, Wyatt Sanford, Easton Carmichael and many more who made major strides this year you likely already know about. But there are also other names you might just be getting familiar with.
Players who forced their way onto the radar
Reinold Navarro, LHP (
No. 21
)
At just 19 years old, Navarro dominated with a 2.96 ERA in 24 apperances (17 starts) across two levels in 2026. Navarro trails just Hunter Barco (
No. 16
) for the top southpaw in the system. His plus fastball and filthy slider helped build a 15.38 K/9.
Like most pitchers, Navarro struggled in his taste of action at High-A Greensboro, known as a hitter’s ballpark. He tallied a 5.59 ERA in 9 2/3 innings after a late-August promotion, but showed plenty in his time at Single-A Bradenton to catch some eyes.
Carlos Tejera, OF (
No. 24
)
Tejera is still a long way from the Major Leagues after just turning 18 years old in July. He moved into the Pirates' Top 30 after the graduation of Valdez in July, and is already 6-foot-2 with plenty of room to fill in.
The left-handed-hitting outfielder dominated his first taste of the Rookie-level Florida Complex League, batting .296 with a .960 OPS and seven walks in nine games. Tejera signed for just $95,000 out of the Dominican Republic, the 12th-highest mark in the Pirates' class. He’s quickly outshining that value.
Connor Wietgrefe, LHP (
No. 29
)
Wietgrefe has always flown under the radar after his selection in the seventh round of the 2024 Draft out of Minnesota. But all the 24-year-old southpaw has done is dominate in professional baseball.
He has posted a 3.12 ERA in 277 1/3 innings over the last three years, and a 3.27 ERA across Double-A Altoona and Triple-A Indianapolis in 2026 has him pushing for a 40-man roster spot. Wietgrefe isn’t a stuff guy with a fastball typically around 91 mph. But he can certainly pitch.
Possible breakouts for 2027
Levi Sterling, RHP (
No. 12
)
Sterling’s numbers don’t jump off the page after producing a 4.92 ERA over his first two professional seasons. But the right-hander has plenty of upside and showed improvement from 2025-26. His walk rate dropped drastically from 6.09 BB/9 to 3.73 while also allowing a .211 opponents' batting average in 108 2/3 innings of his age-19 season.
Sterling earned a promotion to High-A Greensboro still at 19 years old, and he flashed his potential in his final outing on Sept. 2 with nine strikeouts and two solo home runs in five innings, walking just one batter.
Axiel Plaz, C/1B (
No. 7
)
Plaz already had somewhat of a breakout in 2026, batting .305 with 18 homers in 94 games with High-A Greensboro. At 21 years old, Plaz has power at the plate and a rocket arm behind it. A promotion early in 2027 would put Plaz to the test and give him a chance to prove the breakout is for real.
He’s now Pittsburgh’s No. 7 prospect after starting the year at No. 22. Plaz will need to be placed on the 40-man roster to be protected from the Rule 5 Draft.
Biggest question entering next season
Will Hernandez debut in 2027?
Hernandez
told
MLB.com in early July that he hopes to debut in MLB before his 21st birthday, June 28, 2027. A
left oblique injury
later in the month forced him out for the rest of the season, ending his year at High-A Greensboro instead of an expected promotion to Double-A Altoona.
MLB Pipeline’s
top right-handed pitching prospect
still has a chance at making his debut in 2027. But he’ll need to make up for some lost time with even more dominance, and add another weapon to the Pirates' young staff.

led the power parade with three homers, 17 total bases, a 1.308 slugging percentage and 1.770 OPS. The Rockies infield prospect also ranked second in extra-base hits (five) and third in RBIs (six) in a monstrous stretch for the Rafters.

text:
Pirates Insider: Impressive maturity drives catching prospect Easton Carmichael
October 16th, 2026
Jason Mackey
Easton Carmichael hit 20 homers and produced an .825 OPS across two levels in 2026. His 127 hits ranked fourth among qualified Minor League catchers. His 92 RBIs were third among that group and throughout the Pirates’ system.
It was a solid season for the 2025 third-round pick out of the University of Oklahoma. Yet if you ask Carmichael, there was another aspect to his game that meant more than numbers.
“My consistency,” Carmichael said. “I take a lot of pride in that. How I show up and perform … but also who I am as a person, whether it’s going well or not.”
The maturity mental approach comes naturally to Carmichael, who sounds like he’s 22 going on 29 or 30 and has moved quickly through Pittsburgh’s system.
Carmichael’s mother, Julie, is a certified life coach and teaches yoga on the side. His father, Darby, was an accomplished baseball player at Oklahoma, where he later coached.
It’s resulted in ample self-awareness for Easton Carmichael, who played three years at Oklahoma and developed a bunch — something he believed he needed out of high school more so than professional baseball.
“It got to draft day,” Carmichael said, explaining why he chose college over entertaining offers to sign with a club that drafted him.
“I had an opportunity that didn’t make sense for me, whereas if I really wanted to, I probably could have entertained it.
“The money wasn’t right, but I also think that was God’s way of saying, ‘No, you need to go to college and develop that way.’ Ultimately that was the best decision for me.”
And the Pirates, who wanted Carmichael to get some more reps by playing in the Arizona Fall League, in some ways making up for missed time caused by a wrist injury last season but also building volume that will be necessary in the coming years.
Carmichael, who has ascended to the No. 8 spot on MLB Pipeline’s rankings for the Pirates, figures to return to Double-A Altoona in 2027.
MLB Pipeline projects Carmichael’s debut to come in 2028, though that could certainly be sped up given his age, offensive production and an injury or two.
In the meantime, Carmichael isn’t the type to over-worry about his place in the organization. He enjoys being where his feet are and trying to be the same guy every day.
“I take a lot of pride in that because it’s hard,” Carmichael said. “It’s a long season. There are days when you’re tired, and you might not feel great. But I try to be where my feet are and not dwell on anything for too long.”
One thing that has changed for Carmichael involves his weight. Coming out of high school, he was 170 pounds. “Lanky” was how he described himself.
This past season, Carmichael was consistently around 205.
Asked what led to hitting 17 homers as a junior in Norman compared to 13 total his first two seasons, Carmichael said he didn’t drastically change his swing or approach. Mental maturity was about the same.
“I’ve gotten into my grown man body, filling out more,” Carmichael said. “I’ve always known power was there and could come. It was just a matter of when.”
The same for the numbers Carmichael produced in 2026, his first full pro season, amassing 45 extra-base hits, stealing 13 bases and scoring 70 runs.
That patience has been evident in Arizona, too. Despite hitting just .188 with a .485 OPS through four games, Carmichael stayed back on a sinker Thursday and drilled a 103.2 mph double to right field, showcasing that same impressive power.
“I’ve always had a pretty good feel for hitting,” Carmichael said. “Ive been blessed that way.”
Defensively, Carmichael has also made strides this season. Though he only threw out 23.7% of runners (32 of 135), the Pirates have worked with Carmichael on his throwing, using biomechanics to streamline movements and increase velocity.
“We think there’s some meat on the bone there,” Carmichael said.
There’s still some development left for Carmichael, who hit .303 at Greensboro compared to .244 in Altoona. But the Pirates are also working off of an impressive palate, an athletic player with a very mature mindset, something Carmichael directly attributes to his parents.
“They’ve taught me a lot about how to be self-aware and consistent,” Carmichael said. “[Oklahoma baseball coach] Skip Johnson is that way, too. It was very much one pitch at a time.
“I hope my teammates would say that I’m the same guy every day because I do take a lot of pride in my work ethic, consistency and trying to go about things the right way.”

text:
Pirates fans continue to celebrate 1960 World Series with amazing tradition
October 13th, 2026
Jason Mackey
When Brady Peck walked toward Mervis Hall on Pitt’s campus Tuesday afternoon, he was taken aback by the hundreds of people gathered near the Forbes Field wall listening to a baseball game.
A junior from Glen Rock, N.J., Peck asked around and quickly learned about the Pittsburgh tradition, where Pirates fans gather every Oct. 13 to listen to Game 7 of the 1960 World Series, erupting when Bill Mazeroski’s walk-off homer beats the Yankees.
“It’s such a great sense of community,” Peck, 21, said. “I love how it’s right here, on our campus. It’s awesome to see that. Definitely gives you a good feeling before an exam.”
The tradition rolled on as normal as Pirates fans soaked up every ounce of a sun-splashed fall day. At the same time, those gathering did so with heavy hearts after Mazeroski and ElRoy Face passed away in February and Bob Skinner died in May.
Mazeroski and Face were regulars at this event. Mazeroski’s family actually sent a floral wreath that was displayed next to the old-time scoreboard that was added a few years ago.
One of Mazeroski’s cousins, Gary, lives in Aspinwall and made the trip for this year’s event, recalling something he was told growing up about the greatest home run in baseball history and the hysteria that followed.
“Bill later told me that all he was trying to do was find home plate because people mobbed him,” Gary said. “If he didn’t touch home plate, it wouldn’t have counted.”
This event started in 1985, for the 25th anniversary of Maz’s homer, when a Pirates fan named Saul Finkelstein randomly decided to listen to the game near the wall.
It’s grown plenty over time, attracting as many as 1,600 people for the 50th anniversary in 2010 and consistently drawing several hundred fans who bring food and drinks, smoke cigars and reminisce about the Pirates’ rich history.
After Finkelstein got the ball rolling, a group of regulars began calling themselves the “Game 7 Gang," and for the past four decades or so there’s been an organized listening party.
Bob Recker, 83 of Warrendale, has an especially unique perspective on Game 7. He was one of the bat boys for the game and vividly remembers a dejected Casey Stengel walking down the tunnel at Forbes Field.
He also recalled the unique cast of characters who comprised the 1960 Pirates: Roberto Clemente, Maz, Dick Groat, Don Hoak, Smoky Burgess, Vern Law, Bob Friend, Face and many more.
Recker, who was 17 at the time, has seen this tradition evolve and doesn’t want to see it go anywhere as many of its attendees get up there in age.
“It’s a Pittsburgh thing and a part of history that shouldn’t be forgotten,” Recker said. “We need to keep it going.”
Casey Staats of Beaver was doing her part. She took a personal day from work and pushed her young son around in a stroller.
They got some exercise by running around the wall but made sure to return by 3:36 p.m., when Mazeroski took Ralph Terry deep.
“I didn’t think there would be this many people,” Staats said. “We saw a lady handing out I.C. Light like it’s a real ballpark. I wish I would have popped some popcorn. It’s just incredible.”
Mike Imperiale of Jeannette has always wanted to experience the Game 7 listening party. His friends talked it up, the camaraderie, the memories and passion for Pirates baseball on display.
As Imperiale took a break from listening, he couldn’t help but gaze across the street to Posvar Hall, cars lining Roberto & Vera Clemente Drive and how busy Oakland has become.
It’s wild to Imperiale that there was once a ballpark here, where Maz hit the only walk-off, Game 7 homer in World Series history.
“I was only 6 when it happened, but I just remember the city going crazy,” Imperiale said. “It’s a 66-year-old game, and we’re basically in the outfield where the game was being played … it’s just fantastic.”
Which is why Peck was so excited to FaceTime his grandma and share with family members what he learned. He loved the vibes created by the radio broadcast. The passion shown by fans after all these years, too.
It’s why Oct. 13 will always serve multiple purposes in Pittsburgh, to celebrate an historic moment and to educate younger generations about Mazeroski and the Pirates’ rich history.
“It doesn’t surprise me that people still love it,” Gary Mazeroski said. “This place has always been a sports town. It’s really just one big family.”

text:
Pirates Insider: Wyatt Sanford continuing mastery of 'new toy' in Arizona Fall League
October 7th, 2026
Jason Mackey
A few swings into Spring Training, Wyatt Sanford sensed something was different.
When the Pirates drafted Sanford in the second round in 2024, they liked his speed and defense, viewing his left-handed swing as more contact over power ... but also believing that could change over time.
Sanford, 20, did his part over the winter, adding strength to his 5-foot-11, 175-pound frame and revamping the mechanics of his swing. As a result, Sanford increased his OPS more than 200 points (.760 to .963) while barreling toward MLB Pipeline Top 100 status.
“It just felt a little different off the bat, a little different sound,” Sanford said of those early-spring hacks at Pirate City. “It gave me a really good feeling of what’s to come.”
Sanford followed with a stellar season, supplying a stacked High-A Greensboro lineup with speed and all-fields power. It’s also what Sanford has carried with him to the Arizona Fall League, where he’s soaking up extra at-bats and trying to perfect a more powerful stroke after missing two months due to a hand injury.
Sanford, who’s considered Pittsburgh’s fifth-best prospect behind Seth Hernandez, Edward Florentino, Derek Curiel and Murf Gray, homered in the Glendale Desert Dogs’ loss to the Salt River Rafters on Saturday, turning on an inside cutter and launching it over the right-field fence at 100 mph.
In three AFL games so far, Sanford is hitting .364 (4 for 11) with the home run, two RBIs, three runs scored, two walks and three strikeouts. In the process, he’s learned more about himself, his revamped swing and making better decisions when it comes to pitch selection.
“This year was kind of the first time I was able to hit some balls out in BP," Sanford said. “That came with a lot of excitement, getting up to the plate and wanting to swing at a lot of stuff that, looking back, I shouldn’t have swung at.
“That’s one of the big things I’m working on here: staying under control, controlling the zone and still being aggressive.”
Sanford has some things to improve, sure. But he should be plenty proud of the work he did in 2026.
In 77 games between Low-A Bradenton and High-A Greensboro (all but five of those with the Grasshoppers), Sanford hit .282 with 16 doubles, two triples and 19 home runs.
For better year-over-year context, Sanford's slugging percentage jumped from .376 across two levels in 2025 to .546 in 2026. He also had 44 RBI, 77 runs scored and stole 33 bases on 35 attempts.
Sanford struck out 111 times in 363 plate appearances, a rate of roughly 31% that obviously needs to drop.
"He can now swing the bat really fast and hit the ball a long way, something he wasn’t necessarily doing in the past," Pirates general manager Ben Cherington said in August.
“He’s kind of now adapting to that new toy he has and trying to bring the contact back into it. On top of being a really good defensive infielder and athlete and baserunner, we think there’s the makings of a really good player here. He’ll be a fun one to watch in the year or two with how he continues to develop.”
MLB Pipeline estimates Sanford will arrive in the big leagues in 2028, though it probably won’t be at shortstop because of Konnor Griffin. The good news for the Pirates is that Sanford is very athletic and could seemingly adapt to another infield spot or the outfield.
If hits like he did this past season, those moves become even easier.
After Sanford’s homer, he singled twice on Sunday, slapping a breaking ball the opposite way and turning on another heater. It’s a diverse set of tools Sanford didn’t necessarily have during his first pro season, but he’s shown himself to not only be talented but also a quick study.
The hand injury might've disrupted some of that progress, but he’s making up for lost time now in the AFL.
“To see the power really come this year was good to see,” Sanford said. “It was really fun to go out there and play with that extra tool. ... Being super excited having that extra power came with a lot of bad swing decisions early on in the year.
“Before I got hurt, I was trying to find that happy medium. That’s what I’ve been working on here, instead of contact over power or power over contact, making sure that I’m a complete hitter.”

text:
Pirates Insider: Important growth shown by bullpen, catchers in 2026
October 2nd, 2026
Jason Mackey
The last Pirates playoff teams enjoyed production from catchers and elite bullpens. Despite falling short of its ultimate goal, the 2026 group took some important steps toward those goals.
While the bullpen certainly struggled early — only three teams had more blown saves (16) before the All-Star break — the turnaround among Pirates relievers was hard to ignore.
From July 18 on, Pittsburgh amassed the most fWAR (5.3) and had the second-best FIP (3.24) among all MLB bullpens.
Entering 2027, the Pirates have an elite closer (Mason Montgomery) and a top-tier setup man in place — and it’s easy to expect more than Luke Weaver’s 4.96 ERA in 16 1/3 innings with the Pirates.
Around those two could/should be Yohan Ramírez, Carmen Mlodzinski, Wilber Dotel, Lake Bachar, Evan Sisk, Brandon Eisert and a few others — a better starting point than we’ve seen in years.
“Ben [Cherington] did a great job at the deadline of acquiring pitchers,” Pirates pitching coach Bill Murphy said. “That really allowed us to deploy people in different ways.
“[Bachar] opening and doing a number of things allowed us to set other things up. Also the emergence of Mason Montgomery allowed us to solidify that particular position. I think it started with Ben and the work the front office did at the deadline. We’ve just seen our pitchers step into certain roles and really excel.”
Behind the plate, the Pirates should also encouraged by what they saw in 2026, even though there are probably some questions about the shape of the depth chart.
Overall, Pirates catchers were worth a combined 3.4 wins above replacement, per FanGraphs. That ranked ninth in MLB and represents a sizable improvement over how Pirates catchers fared in 2025 (1.0 fWAR, 25th).
Rafael Flores Jr. was the big story there, the right-handed hitter improving behind the plate and homering 11 times in 148 at-bats while producing an .858 OPS. Between Flores, Henry Davis, Endy Rodriguez, Joey Bart and Shawn Ross, Pirates catchers hit 29 homers, fifth-most in MLB.
“We see it as a strength going forward,” Pirates manager Ben Cherington said of the team’s catching depth. “I just hope those three continue to challenge each other.”
Five storylines
1.
Montgomery began the season as a project lefty, an opener who only occasionally saw leverage inning.
Montgomery finished it by impersonating Aroldis Chapman or Josh Hader. Among the numbers:
• Montgomery’s scoreless streak of 24 2/3 was the longest for a Pirates reliever since 1989.
• The most fWAR (1.8) and second-best FIP (1.39) among MLB relievers with at least 20 innings pitched after the All-Star break.
• Had it not been for five starts, Montgomery’s 105 strikeouts would’ve been the third-most for a Pirates reliever in franchise history.
“I don't think he's faking his way to that performance,” Cherington said. “It's pretty real.”
And spectacular.
2.
Yohan Ramírez was also a tremendous story … and important because he’ll be back.
The effervescent reliever enjoyed his first full MLB season and produced career-bests across the board: 66 games, 85.0 innings, 2.86 ERA, 1.2 fWAR and 102 strikeouts.
Not bad for someone who was designated for assignment nine times prior to this season. Ramirez earned himself regular work in Pittsburgh, though it came a variety of ways, from one appearances as an opener to multiple innings, fireman stuff and leverage.
Montgomery and Ramirez made the Pirates just the sixth team in the Modern Era (since 1901) to employ two pitchers who appeared in 65 or more games and notched 100 or more strikeouts in the same season.
3.
Flipping over to catchers … Flores was one of the Pirates’ best stories this year, regardless of position. He struggled defensively and, for a stretch, looked more like a future first baseman.
He kept working, changed his setup and improved a bunch, throwing out seven of the final 22 (31.8%) runners who tried to steal against him.
Davis is easily the best defender of the group. However, Flores’ 11 homers and .858 OPS in 47 games made it a no-brainer to give him the bulk of the reps.
Flores also fared well against lefties (.924 OPS), which is something the Pirates need to balance out their lineup.
4.
Weird spot with Davis. Only five catchers in either league were worth more defensive runs saved (FanGraphs) than Davis, who threw out 45.9% (20 of 37) of runners trying to steal.
Davis improved a lot with ABS challenges during the second half and excels as a game-planner and pitch-caller. But he’s also hitting just .178 with a .565 OPS through 958 MLB plate appearances.
Pretty much the opposite of what was expected of Davis when he was drafted.
5.
The focus was on Luke Weaver among the Pirates adds at the trade deadline. But Bachar was a sneaky great pickup.
Bachar excelled as an opener, pitching to a 2.25 ERA in 16 innings during his Pirates starts. The right-hander worked 86 2/3 innings between Miami and Pittsburgh while producing a 3.43 ERA with 93 strikeouts in 86 2/3 innings.
The spin stuff was sharp, with Bachar allowing a batting average against under .200 and producing a whiff rate of at least 39.7% on his slider and curveball, which he threw a combined 40.7% of the time.

Four numbers
1:71:
ERA for Ramirez in 40 games (52 2/3 innings) from June on.
102:
wRC+ for Pirates catchers, their best such mark since 2018.
2.81:
Gregory Soto’s ERA from July-September, spanning 32 innings. The veteran lefty had a 13.50 ERA in 7 1/3 June innings before rebounding.
18:
Saves for Montgomery since he notched his first one on July 11, tired with Emilio Pagan and David Bednar for the MLB lead during that time.
Three questions
1.
What happens with Carmen Mlodzinski? Cherington said they don’t need to define his role now, and the Pirates GM isn’t wrong. But it would make sense to have that conversation relatively soon in case Mlodzinski and the Pirates don’t agree on how he should be used.
If that’s as a reliever, great. Mlodzinski has a career 2.66 ERA in that spot and would help any bullpen in baseball. But if he insists on starting, it could make sense for the Pirates to try and recoup some of that value.
2.
Can Rodriguez stay healthy?
When he was in the lineup, Rodriguez hit .267 and had an .840 OPS in 45 games. But he also couldn’t stay healthy, suffering from hip and glute issues that ended his season.
Feels like catching might not be in the cards for Rodriguez, but could the Pirates use his bat somewhere else?
3.
Who do they add? With Soto’s contract expiring, the Pirates should have at least one position to back-fill. It could be a lefty setup man, or they could entrust those duties to Evan Sisk and Brandon Eisert, who pitched well at different times.
Same as ever, it’s the easiest thing to improve year-to-year. But with Montgomery, Weaver and a few others established, the Pirates could get creative.
Two predictions
1.
Weaver returns to his previous form. OK, not a hot take considering he had a 1.84 ERA in 42 games with the Mets before the trade. Over the past three seasons, Weaver ranks 21st in fWAR (2.9) among relievers with at least 150 innings pitched.
The right-hander closed the season with four scoreless outings, while his four-seamer was among the most productive pitches (.192 BA against, run value of 8) on the staff.
2.
The Pirates move on from either Mlodzinski or Davis this offseason. They’re not related situations. Merely things the team must consider considering in-house options and potential outside interest.
One quote
“He’s been fantastic. A guy who can swing it like that, who can catch and play first, he’s a really valuable guy. It’s been fun to see what he’s done.” — Ryan O’Hearn on Flores.

title: Pirates Arizona Fall League overview 2026 | SCOTTSDALE, Ariz. -- If things continue to develop as planned, the Pirates will have to decide which best friend will be their big league shortstop. Konnor Griffin might have the gig now, but his buddy Wyatt Sanford isn’t that far off from trying to lay claim to the premium position
text:
'Finding a happy medium': Pirates prospect Sanford using Fall League to become a more complete hitter
October 8th, 2026
Jonathan Mayo
SCOTTSDALE, Ariz. -- If things continue to develop as planned, the Pirates will have to decide which best friend will be their big league shortstop. Konnor Griffin might have the gig now, but his buddy
Wyatt Sanford
isn’t
that
far off from trying to lay claim to the premium position in Pittsburgh.
“He was my first roommate in pro ball when we were both drafted,” Sanford said. “Seeing what he’s done throughout his career so far is just truly amazing and truly incredible, and I'm very happy for him. I think the big piece I take away from him is how he handles himself off the field.
“It reminds me at the end of the day that teammates remember how good of a dude you are, and it just allows me to realize ... 0-for-4, 4-for-4, just be the same guy, you know, be the same guy that shows up in the locker room every day, excited to come to work and excited to play.”

So maybe there won’t be a friend rift when Sanford is ready -- he has played some second base just in case -- and he’s still a couple of rungs behind his Draft mate. Taken a round after Griffin in 2024, injuries have slowed Sanford’s progress some. The
Pirates’ No. 5 prospect
missed time with a groin injury in 2025, then spent the offseason working on conditioning to avoid muscle-related issues like that.
Sanford did that in 2026, but was limited to just 77 games after suffering a broken hand when he was hit by a pitch. That’s one of the big reasons he’s playing for the Glendale Desert Dogs in the Arizona Fall League, to make up for lost reps on both sides of the ball.
“That was pretty brutal,” Sanford said. “The offseason focus was making sure none of the muscle stuff happens during the season, never would I have thought that I'd be getting hit in the hand and missing two months, but here we are.
“It's funny, every year for Spring Training, we get a hand guard and I was always like, ‘Man, I never need that.’ And of course now, for the rest of my career, I'll be wearing one.”
While the 20-year-old wouldn’t have been on the Griffin express to Pittsburgh, he almost certainly would have made it to Double-A this year. Coming out of high school with a reputation as a contact-first hitter, Sanford’s offseason work to add strength showed up and then some, with 10 homers over the first two months before the injury.

“And just a lot of eating in the offseason, that's been a big help too, so definitely going to do that again this offseason,” Sanford said with a smile. “I don't think I was expecting that at all. I think the first day of Spring Training, the first day we took BP, it just felt a little bit different off the bat, a little bit different sound, and it kind of just gave me a really good feeling of what's to come. I've always been a contact-over-power hitter and so to see the power really come this year was really good to see, and it was really fun to go out there and play with that extra tool.”
That new extra tool did come with extra swing-and-miss, however. Sanford admits the excitement of being able to impact the baseball led to some poor swing decisions and a 32.5 percent strikeout rate in April and May. He hit nine more homers over August and September when he got back with High-A Greensboro, but started to figure out how to get to that pop without selling out too much for it, cutting the K rate to 28.7 percent during that stretch.

“That is very important, and I think that's one of the biggest things I'm working on when I'm down here, just refining that approach and getting back to the approach I had when I was a contact-over-power guy,” Sanford said. “Before I got hurt, I was trying to find the groove of finding a happy medium. I’m working on that when I'm down here and just making sure I'm a complete hitter.”
